content.title: About
content.content: Bulgur is a pre-cooked, dried, and coarsely ground wheat of the hard varieties (triticale). It is widely used in Middle Eastern, Mediterranean and Caucasian cuisines. Bulgur has a light nutty flavor, pleasant texture and cooks quickly.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bulgur dates back to ancient Egypt where it was used in ceremonial dishes.
Unlike couscous, bulgur is not steamed before drying, preserving more nutrients.
It comes in several grinds: fine (for couscous), medium (for tabbouleh) and coarse (for soups).
Bulgur is often used as a rice or couscous substitute in diet meals.
When kept dry, it can be stored for up to 2 years.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Both soluble and insoluble fiber support digestion and promote satiety.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Complex carbohydrates provide a slow, steady release of energy, helpful for blood‑sugar control.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B3 and B6 vitamins aid carbohydrate metabolism and support the nervous system.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Bulgur supplies iron, magnesium, phosphorus and zinc, important for blood, bones and immunity.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: It contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Bulgur is made from wheat, so it is unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: It contains phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption when consumed in excess.

items.title: Food allergies
items.content: Rarely, wheat‑sensitive individuals may experience an allergic reaction.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bulgur can be used as a side dish, added to salads (tabbouleh), soups, meat fillings and patties. Typically the grains are rinsed, soaked for 15‑30 minutes, then boiled 10‑15 minutes until tender.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store bulgur in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from moisture and light. For long‑term storage, keep it in the refrigerator.

content.title: About
content.content: The beef and cheese burrito is a Mexican dish consisting of a large flour or corn tortilla wrapped around a filling of sautéed beef, melted cheese, rice, beans, and spices. Served hot, it is often accompanied by salsa, guacamole, and sour cream.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Burritos originated in northern Mexico in the early 20th century as a portable meal for workers.
Traditional Mexican burritos are modest in size, while U.S. versions are frequently much larger.
The combination of beef and cheese provides a rich umami flavor prized by meat lovers.
Beef‑cheese burritos often include chipotle or ground cumin to boost aroma.
Because of their high protein content, burritos are popular among athletes as a hearty post‑workout meal.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Beef and cheese are excellent sources of complete protein, essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Iron source
items.content: Beef supplies heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheese contributes calcium needed for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Energy‑dense carbs
items.content: Rice and beans provide quick‑release carbohydrates, useful for fueling physical activity.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef offers vitamin B12, while beans provide folate, both important for nervous system health and blood formation.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Cheese and beef can be high in saturated fats, so individuals with cardiovascular concerns should limit portion size.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Prepared sauces and cheese often contain added salt, which may raise blood pressure.

items.title: Dairy allergy or lactose intolerance
items.content: People with milk protein allergy or lactose intolerance should choose dairy‑free cheese alternatives.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: A burrito is calorie‑rich; overconsumption can contribute to weight gain.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Burritos are conveniently eaten by hand, often cut in half. Serve with salsa, guacamole, sour cream, or fresh cilantro. For a lighter version, use a whole‑grain tortilla and reduce the amount of cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store a prepared burrito in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze it wrapped in plastic; reheat in the microwave or on a skillet before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Ready‑to‑eat oat bran cereal is made from whole oat bran that has been dried and pressed into light flakes. It is rich in fiber, B‑vitamins, and minerals, offering a mild nutty flavor and a convenient quick‑breakfast option.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oat bran contains more dietary fiber than regular rolled oats.
Bran is the outer layer of the oat grain that is removed during the production of standard oat flakes.
Minimal heat processing preserves most of the nutrients in ready‑to‑eat oat bran flakes.
Oats have been cultivated for over 5,000 years, making them one of the oldest grain crops.
Bran is often used in diet plans to help lower cholesterol levels.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Heart‑healthy
items.content: Beta‑glucans in bran can reduce LDL‑cholesterol, supporting cardiovascular health.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2, and B6 aid energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Bran provides magnesium, iron, and phosphorus, essential for bone and muscle health.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: The fiber slows carbohydrate absorption, helping control appetite and glucose spikes.

items.title: Oat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to oats or oat proteins.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Bran contains phytic acid, which can reduce the absorption of certain minerals when consumed in excess.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: A sudden increase in fiber intake may cause bloating or loose stools.

items.title: Gluten cross‑contamination
items.content: Although oats are naturally gluten‑free, they are often processed on equipment shared with wheat; choose certified gluten‑free products if you have celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy oat bran flakes dry, or add milk, yogurt, or plant‑based milk. Mix with fresh fruit, nuts, honey, or use in smoothies, baked goods, and as a topping for salads for a quick, nutritious meal.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the flakes in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from light. For longer shelf life, keep them refrigerated to prevent fat oxidation. Discard if they develop a rancid smell or visible mold.

content.title: About
content.content: Chia seeds are edible seeds of the plant Salvia hispanica, native to Mexico and Guatemala. They are tiny (about 2 mm), oval‑shaped, and dark brown to black. Chia is nutrient‑dense, forms a gel when mixed with liquid, and is widely used in health‑focused diets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chia was a staple food for the ancient Aztec and Maya civilizations, valued for its energy‑boosting properties.
The seeds can absorb up to 12 times their weight in water, creating a gelatinous texture popular in smoothies and puddings.
Chia is not a nut, making it suitable for people with nut allergies.
In the 1990s, chia gained popularity as a “superfood” across Europe and the United States.
Chia is rich in omega‑3 fatty acids in the form of alpha‑linolenic acid (ALA).

items.title: Rich in omega‑3
items.content: Chia provides alpha‑linolenic acid, which supports heart and vascular health.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: About 20 % of the seed’s weight is protein, beneficial for muscle and tissue maintenance.

items.title: Loaded with antioxidants
items.content: Phenolic compounds and quercetin protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports bone health
items.content: Chia contains calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus, essential for strong bones.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to chia seeds.

items.title: Digestive issues
items.content: High fiber intake can cause bloating, gas, or diarrhea if not accompanied by adequate fluid consumption.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Because of its omega‑3 content, chia may enhance the effects of anticoagulant drugs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add chia seeds to smoothies, yogurt, oatmeal, or baked goods, or make a pudding by soaking them in milk or water for 10‑15 minutes. They also work as a thickener for sauces and dressings. Sprinkle them on salads or use in energy bars.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store chia seeds in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long‑term storage, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent fat oxidation.

nutritional-powder-mix-eas-whey-protein-.title: Nutritional Powder Mix (EAS Whey Protein Powder)

content.title: About
content.content: The Nutritional Powder Mix EAS Whey Protein Powder is a high‑quality whey protein designed to support muscle growth, post‑workout recovery, and increase daily protein intake. The powder mixes easily with water, milk, or juice and has a pleasant flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whey protein is rapidly absorbed, delivering a quick influx of amino acids to muscles.
EAS was one of the first brands to add digestive enzymes to protein blends for better tolerance.
The formula is low in fat and carbs, making it suitable for low‑calorie diets.
Contains added enzymes (protease, lactase) to improve digestion.
First released in the 1990s, it has earned a strong reputation among athletes.

items.title: Supports muscle growth
items.content: A complete profile of essential amino acids, including BCAAs, promotes muscle‑protein synthesis after training.

items.title: Accelerates recovery
items.content: Whey quickly replenishes glycogen stores and aids repair of damaged muscle fibers.

items.title: Helps weight management
items.content: High protein content increases satiety, helping to reduce overall calorie intake.

items.title: Boosts immunity
items.content: Glutamine and other immune‑supporting components help strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Easy digestion
items.content: Added enzymes facilitate digestion and reduce the risk of stomach discomfort.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: The product contains whey protein, which can trigger allergic reactions in individuals with dairy sensitivities.

items.title: Excessive protein intake
items.content: Consuming too much protein may strain kidneys and liver, especially in people with pre‑existing conditions.

items.title: Artificial sweeteners
items.content: Some versions include sucralose or aspartame, which may be undesirable for sensitive consumers.

items.title: Possible gastrointestinal issues
items.content: Large doses can cause bloating, gas, or diarrhea in some individuals.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Mix one scoop (≈30 g) with 250–300 ml of water, milk, or fruit juice. Take 1–2 servings per day, preferably post‑workout and/or between meals to boost overall protein intake.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place with the package tightly sealed. Keep moisture and direct sunlight away. For extended shelf life, transfer to the refrigerator to maintain freshness.

pasta-whole-grain-with-tomato-based-sauc.title: Whole Grain Pasta with Tomato Sauce and Seafood

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain pasta with tomato sauce and seafood is a home recipe (3659). Whole grain pasta retains bran and germ, increasing fiber and micronutrient content. The tomato sauce, made from ripe tomatoes, provides lycopene and vitamin C, while seafood (shrimp, mussels, squid) adds protein, omega‑3 fatty acids, and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole grain pasta has a lower glycemic index than refined white pasta.
Tomatoes used in the sauce are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that supports heart health.
Seafood is one of the best natural sources of iodine, essential for thyroid function.
Making the sauce at home lets you control salt and sugar levels, making the dish healthier.
In Italy, whole‑grain pasta is traditionally called "pasta integrale".

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole grain pasta provides soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion and stable blood glucose.

items.title: Plant protein source
items.content: Whole grain flour supplies about 12 g of protein per 100 g, beneficial for vegetarians.

items.title: Lycopene and vitamin C
items.content: Tomato sauce is rich in lycopene and vitamin C, which boost immunity and have anti‑inflammatory effects.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Seafood delivers EPA and DHA omega‑3s, important for heart and brain health.

items.title: Minerals (iodine, zinc, iron)
items.content: Shrimp and mussels provide iodine, zinc, and iron, essential for metabolism and immune function.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to shrimp, mussels, or squid, ranging from skin rash to anaphylaxis.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Tomato sauce often contains added salt; monitor sodium intake, especially for people with hypertension.

items.title: Foodborne toxins
items.content: Improperly stored seafood can develop histamine or other toxins that cause food poisoning.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Whole grain pasta contains gluten and is unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pasta hot, topped with the tomato‑seafood sauce. Garnish with fresh basil, grated Parmesan, or a drizzle of olive oil. For a lighter texture, cook the pasta al dente.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep dry pasta in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked sauce and seafood should be refrigerated and consumed within 2‑3 days, or frozen in a sealed container for up to one month.

content.title: About
content.content: Mashed potato with gravy is a classic restaurant side dish made from boiled potatoes that are whipped into a smooth, creamy consistency and served under a rich meat or vegetable gravy. The mash is typically enriched with butter, milk or cream, giving it a velvety texture and savory flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mashed potatoes became popular in Europe in the 17th century when milk and butter were added to improve taste.
Gravy variations—meat, mushroom, or vegetable—provide diverse flavor profiles across cuisines.
Restaurants often use high‑starch potato varieties to achieve an especially airy mash.
Mashed potatoes with gravy are commonly paired with steaks, meatballs, and baked fish.
Traditional preparation involves passing the potatoes through a sieve or press for a perfectly smooth texture.

items.title: Rich in potassium
items.content: Potatoes are a good source of potassium, which supports healthy blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Vitamin C source
items.content: Potatoes contain vitamin C, an antioxidant that helps strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Energy provider
items.content: The mash supplies quick‑digesting carbohydrates, useful for replenishing energy after physical activity.

items.title: Enhanced nutrient bioavailability
items.content: Cooking and mashing increase the absorption of certain vitamins and minerals.

items.title: Digestive ease
items.content: The soft texture is gentle on the stomach, making it suitable for children and those with chewing difficulties.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Butter and cream added to the mash raise its calorie count, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Gravy often contains salt; people with hypertension should opt for low‑sodium versions.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: If the gravy or mash includes milk or cream, individuals with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Potatoes have a high glycemic index, which can cause rapid spikes in blood sugar.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the mash hot as a side to meat, fish, or vegetable dishes. Garnish with fresh herbs, grated cheese, or fried onions. For a lighter version, replace cream with low‑fat milk.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep prepared mashed potatoes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. When reheating, add a splash of milk or cream to restore creaminess. Freeze only the plain mash; reheat and add gravy separately if needed.

tea-iced-brewed-green-decaffeinated-pre-.title: Iced Green Tea, Decaffeinated, Pre‑sweetened with Low‑Calorie Sweetener

content.title: About
content.content: This iced green tea is brewed, then cooled and sweetened with a low‑calorie sweetener. It retains the fresh, grassy flavor of green tea while being caffeine‑free, making it suitable for evening consumption.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green tea is rich in polyphenols, which have antioxidant properties.
Decaffeination is usually performed by steam processing, preserving most beneficial compounds.
Low‑calorie sweeteners such as stevia allow sweetness with minimal calories.
Iced tea is often served with a slice of lemon or a sprig of mint to enhance flavor.
In Japan, ready‑to‑drink cold green teas are a popular beverage.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Polyphenols in green tea help neutralize free radicals, supporting cellular health.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Regular green tea consumption is associated with improved lipid profiles and lower blood pressure.

items.title: Hydration aid
items.content: A caffeine‑free cold beverage contributes to fluid balance, especially in warm weather.

items.title: Low calorie content
items.content: Sweetened with a low‑calorie sweetener, the drink provides minimal calories, useful for weight management.

items.title: No nervous system stimulation
items.content: Absence of caffeine makes it safe for children, pregnant individuals, and those sensitive to stimulants.

items.title: Tea allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to tea components.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Green tea contains oxalates, which in excess may contribute to kidney stone formation.

items.title: Artificial sweeteners
items.content: Some individuals may experience digestive discomfort from certain low‑calorie sweeteners (e.g., maltitol).

content.title: How to Enjoy
content.content: Serve the iced tea chilled; add a lemon or lime wedge or a sprig of mint if desired. It pairs well with light snacks, fruit, and salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the beverage refrigerated at 0 °C–4 °C. Once opened, consume within 3–5 days. Do not freeze, as it may affect texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Thousand Island dressing is a classic American condiment made from a base of mayonnaise, ketchup, and finely chopped pickled vegetables. It has a sweet‑tangy flavor with a hint of spice and is commonly used on salads, sandwiches, and burgers.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name comes from the Thousand Islands region between the United States and Canada, where the sauce is said to have originated.
Traditional recipes include minced cornichons, onion, green pepper, and sometimes anchovies.
Many variations exist: some add mustard, Worcestershire sauce, or hot sauce.
It is a staple topping for the classic club sandwich and shrimp cocktail.
In Russia the sauce became popular in the 1990s as a ready‑to‑use salad dressing.

items.title: Source of vitamin E
items.content: The mayonnaise base provides vitamin E, an antioxidant that helps protect cells.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Plant‑based oils supply monounsaturated fatty acids that are heart‑friendly.

items.title: Rich in lycopene
items.content: Tomato ketchup adds lycopene, a compound linked to reduced oxidative stress.

items.title: May provide probiotics (when fermented pickles are used)
items.content: Fermented pickles can contribute beneficial bacteria for gut health.

items.title: Low sugar when homemade
items.content: By controlling the amount of ketchup, added sugar can be kept to a minimum.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Mayonnaise contains eggs, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The creamy base makes the dressing calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Sugar and sodium
items.content: Ketchup and pickles add sugar and salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Preservatives in commercial versions
items.content: Store‑bought dressings may contain artificial additives that some people prefer to avoid.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use Thousand Island dressing as a salad dressing, a burger or sandwich sauce, a dip for vegetables or seafood, or stir it into potato salad or egg dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the dressing refrigerated in a sealed container for 2‑3 weeks. Discard if you notice off‑flavors, discoloration, or mold.
